props.title: What Have I Done to Deserve This?
props.initialSlug: Desperate housewife's chaotic life spirals into madness

sections.content: Pedro Almodóvar's early masterpiece What Have I Done to Deserve This? perfectly captures the chaotic energy of post-Franco Madrid through a darkly comic lens. Carmen Maura delivers a tour-de-force performance as Gloria, an overworked housewife driven to her limits by a dysfunctional family and grinding poverty. The film established Almodóvar's signature blend of melodrama and pitch-black humor that would later flourish in Women on the Verge of a Nervous Breakdown (1988) and All About My Mother (1999). Like Federico Fellini's Juliet of the Spirits (1965), it uses surreal elements to explore female psychological distress.

movies.slug: A complex tale of passion and obsession in Madrid's artistic community

sections.content: The film's portrayal of working-class Spanish life draws from Italian Neorealism while adding distinctly Spanish touches and surreal flourishes. Like Vittorio De Sica's Bicycle Thieves (1948), it depicts economic hardship without sacrificing humanity or humor. Gloria's struggles with her family - including a husband obsessed with German porn, a son who deals drugs, and another who sleeps with older men - reflect the social upheaval of post-Franco Spain. The inclusion of a telepathic daughter and a pet lizard adds Almodóvar's characteristic outlandish touches.

The film's feminist undertones emerge through Gloria's gradual awakening and rebellion against patriarchal structures. This theme would become central to Almodóvar's later works like Volver (2006) and Pain and Glory (2019). The director's use of bold colors and melodramatic plotting draws from Douglas Sirk's 1950s melodramas while subverting their conventions with modern sexual politics and dark comedy. sections.content: What Have I Done to Deserve This? helped establish the "Movida Madrileña" movement, Spain's cultural renaissance following Franco's death. Along with films like Pepi, Luci, Bom (1980) and Labyrinth of Passion (1982), it captured the energy and freedom of newly democratic Spain. The film's frank treatment of sexuality, drug use, and family dysfunction broke taboos and helped pave the way for contemporary Spanish cinema.
